analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare hospitals to set nurse staffing plans with enough registered nurses for safe patient care.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action in the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital that takes Medicare patients to create a written nurse staffing plan, drafted by a committee where a majority of members are frontline nurses, aimed at having enough registered nurses on every unit and every shift for safe care. It would also have let nurses refuse unsafe assignments, protected whistleblowers from retaliation, forced hospitals to post daily staffing numbers publicly, and set fines for violations. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients would gain, because each Medicare hospital would have to set a staffing plan with enough registered nurses on every unit and every shift to deliver safe care, and post daily staffing numbers the public could see [S3]. Frontline nurses would gain a guaranteed seat (a majority of the committee) writing those staffing plans, the right to refuse assignments they are not trained for or that violate the plan, and whistleblower protection against retaliation for complaining about staffing [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Each Medicare hospital would have to implement a hospital-wide staffing plan requiring an appropriate number of registered nurses in every unit on every shift, aimed at safe, quality patient care

A nurse staffing committee, with at least 55% of members being direct-care registered nurses rather than managers or administrators, would write and annually re-evaluate the plan, giving frontline nurses a formal say in staffing decisions

Nurses could refuse assignments that violate the staffing plan or that they lack the training to handle safely, and hospitals could not retaliate against patients or employees who complain — with court remedies including reinstatement, back pay, and $5,000 in damages for patients

Hospitals would have to post daily staffing numbers in a visible place and report nursing quality data to the government for publication on the Hospital Compare website, so patients could compare hospitals on staffing

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals that treat Medicare patients would bear the cost of hiring more registered nurses, running nurse staffing committees, posting daily staffing information, and reporting quality data to the federal government, backed by fines of at least $10,000 per knowing violation [S3]. Higher staffing costs could be passed on to insurers and patients through hospital prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no dedicated federal funding; hospitals would absorb the cost of higher registered-nurse staffing, and critics of such mandates argue the expense could pressure hospital budgets, be passed to insurers and patients, or strain rural hospitals — which the bill gives four years instead of two to comply

The approach relies on committees and plans rather than fixed nurse-to-patient ratios, so staffing requirements would be self-determined by each hospital's own committee and enforcement would depend on federal complaint procedures and penalties

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is higher hospital labor costs versus fewer preventable patient harms. The bill's own findings cite research linking higher registered-nurse staffing to lower rates of falls, infections, medication errors, and death, and note that inadequate staffing contributed to 24% of unanticipated patient deaths or injuries [S3]. It also cites the cost to hospitals of replacing a nurse at more than 100% of annual salary, meaning chronic understaffing carries its own large cost in turnover [S3]. A hospital-by-hospital committee approach is more flexible but less enforceable than fixed ratios, and no funding was provided. The bill never advanced far enough for these trade-offs to be debated publicly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and sat there until the two-year Congress expired, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 25, 2011 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day
The Finance Committee took no further action; the full action history shows only introduction and referral, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013
The bill attracted only one cosponsor in two years

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals are better off: no staffing plan requirements, no staffing committees, no public posting of daily nurse counts, and no fines were ever imposed. Patients and nurses gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that avoided new staffing rules

for.name: Sen. Daniel Inouye
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the referred bill without a hearing, markup, or floor vote for the full two-year Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough to produce a vote, so no roll-call record exists; it had one Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill would have conditioned Medicare participation on adopting nurse staffing plans, hiring enough registered nurses per shift, running committees dominated by frontline nurses, posting daily staffing counts publicly, and facing civil fines of $10,000 or more per violation. This directly raises hospitals' largest labor cost; the bill died before any of it took effect.

industries.industry: Nursing labor unions and staffing agencies
industries.note: The bill would have barred hospitals from replacing registered nurses with lower-paid aides for direct care duties covered by staffing plans and required input from nurses' exclusive representatives, strengthening the role of organized nursing in hospital staffing decisions.

Plans would need adjustable minimum registered-nurse numbers and could not use those minimums as caps, pushing hospitals to hire more RNs; the bill's findings cite heavy nurse burnout and turnover under current conditions.
